meta.title: Who really said "We suffer more often in imagination than in reality"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, it’s Seneca. The line is Epistle 13.4 of his Moral Letters to Lucilius (c. 65 CE), Richard Gummere’s Loeb translation of the Latin “saepius opinione quam re laboramus.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We suffer more often in imagination than in reality'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Seneca — Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 13 (‘On Groundless Fears’), section 4, c. 65 CE. We traced the Latin original and the Loeb translation.

answer.sourceLine: From Seneca’s Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter 13, ‘On Groundless Fears,’ §4. The English is Richard M. Gummere’s Loeb translation of the Latin “saepius opinione quam re laboramus” — a genuine, locatable primary source.

source.excerpt: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
trail: The line traces to Seneca’s Letter 13 in the Gummere translation, where it closes the opening argument of ‘On Groundless Fears.’
The Latin original — “saepius opinione quam re laboramus” — is confirmed in The Latin Library’s text of Epistle 13.4.
Wikiquote lists it in its sourced section, with Latin and translation — not under ‘Misattributed’ or ‘Disputed.’
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular one-liner drops the first half of the sentence
source.excerptNote: The Latin original reads: “Plura sunt, Lucili, quae nos terrent quam quae premunt, et saepius opinione quam re laboramus.” The word opinione (opinion / apprehension) is what Gummere renders as “imagination”; other translators give “we suffer more often in apprehension than in reality.”

author.bio: Lucius Annaeus Seneca (Seneca the Younger) was a Roman Stoic philosopher, dramatist, and statesman who served as tutor and later advisor to the emperor Nero. His Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium — 124 letters on how to live — are among the most influential works of practical Stoicism. Ordered by Nero to take his own life in 65 CE, he died as his philosophy counseled.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Letter 13 is Seneca’s essay on groundless fear. The point of the line is not that suffering is unreal, but that anticipation multiplies it: the mind rehearses disasters that never arrive, and pays interest on debts it may never owe.
“We are in the habit of exaggerating, or imagining, or anticipating sorrow,” he writes a few sentences later — a diagnosis modern cognitive therapy would recognize two thousand years on.
